newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea Kia creditors take tough stance on bailout.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea Kia creditors take tough stance on bailout.

text.p: South Korean creditor banks delayed for the second time on Friday a decision on bailing out eighth-ranked Kia Group in what analysts said signalled a toughening stance towards the troubled conglomerate.
Creditors said they could reach no decision on Friday because of continuing disagreements with Kia management over core issues. They said they would meet again on August 4.
The most contentious issue appeared to be creditors' demand that Kia executives, including group chairman Kim Sun-hong, resign before they extended a bailout programme.
Kwon Woo-ha, a senior executive at main creditor Korea First Bank, told a news conference creditors were disappointed with Kia.
"Our demand has not been met at all. We still want the Kia management to resign unconditionally," Kwon said.
But the Kia chairman was defiant when he met with reporters.
"I cannot accept creditors' demand for my unconditional resignation," Kim said.
Analysts questioned the creditors' hardened attitude toward Kia, whose flagship is Kia Motors Corp.

Huh Ghang, an auto industry analyst at Hyundai Securities, said the demands of creditor banks were especially severe when compared to their treatment of the only two other South Korean business groups put under bank protection, Jinro and Dainong.
Creditors accepted those groups' self-rescue plans but rejected Kia's as not going far enough, he said.

Before Wednesday's creditor meeting, Kia announced harsher self-rescue measures, including a cut in the number of its domestic units to five from the current 28 through sell-offs, mergers and spin-offs.
Kia also said Asia Motors would sell off part of its assets before being absorbed by Kia Motors to serve as assembly plants.
"It's too harsh for creditors to ask for Kim's unconditional resignation even before granting any real help," Huh said.
The attitude of the creditors suggested they would prefer a third-party takeover of Kia by a healthy group, he said.
"Banks seem to believe a takeover would make it easier for them to get their loans repaid without having to assume any big losses," Huh said.
Prior to Friday's meeting analysts had said a move by the country's two largest carmakers to inject cash into Kia's troubled steelmaking unit would help the group in its negotiations with creditors.

Kia announced on Thursday that Hyundai Motor, the country's largest carmaker, and unlisted Daewoo Motor Co had agreed in principle to buy stakes in Kia Steel Co, a speciality steelmaker that is one of Kia's weakest affiliates.

Under the agreement, Hyundai, Daewoo and Kia would form a consortium with each having equal stakes to run Kia Steel. A Kia statement said the three companies had agreed to start working-level negotiations to work out details.

Creditors put Kia Group under their protection on July 15 after determining that Kia affiliates were on the verge of defaulting on debt payments. Kia's debts totalled 9.5 trillion won ($10.6 billion) as of the end of May.
